R_H1.passageTitle: How children travel to school in England

passages.label: A
passages.text: A chart about school transport can show a number of things immediately. The English National Travel Survey asks families to write down their journeys over seven days. The Department for Transport brings these trips together in a report. A table can then show which groups use a bus, go on foot or travel in other ways.

passages.label: B
passages.text: For children aged five to ten, walking was the most common way to travel. Fifty-one per cent of trips were made on foot, and forty-three per cent were by car. About two per cent were made by children who take a local bus to school. About one per cent were made by children who ride a bicycle. The percentage refers to trips in the survey.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Older children travelled differently. Among pupils aged eleven to sixteen, thirty-seven per cent of trips were made on foot. Thirty per cent were by car and eighteen per cent by local bus. Two per cent used a bicycle. The lower walking percentage does not tell us what every older child would prefer.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Distance changes the pattern. For pupils aged eleven to sixteen, walking was most common when the journey was under one mile. For trips of two to under five miles, many families drive or use a bus. For trips of five miles or more, the bus had the largest share. A short route and a long route therefore produce a different result.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Some families wanted safer roads with less traffic or safer places to cross. Others said that children had to spend too much time walking. The report gives a group result. It does not settle each person's opinion of the best route. A teacher can ask pupils which type of transport they prefer and create a chart for the class to compare with the national figures. The traffic near a school, the pavement and the risk of an accident also affect choices. In areas with gridlock, a short walk may be faster than a trip in a car. In the countryside, the road to school may be long.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Before using a transport service in London, a visitor may choose between travelling on foot, taking a taxi or going by bicycle and paying a fare on public transport. For someone who prefers to ride a bus or to take a train, Transport for London explains that passengers may pay with an Oyster card or a contactless card or device. The advice includes the London Underground, the city's metro system.

passages.label: B
passages.text: On the Underground and most rail services, a passenger touches a yellow reader at the start of a journey and again at the final stage. The passenger must touch out even when a station gate is open, and some stations have no gate. At those stations, a free-standing reader is provided near an entrance, exit or platform. Following the steps helps a passenger spend only the correct fare.

passages.label: C
passages.text: On a bus or tram, the reader must be touched at the outset of the journey, but a second touch when getting off can create an additional charge. This is the opposite of rail and Underground travel, where the system uses a touch at each end to work out the correct fare.

passages.label: D
passages.text: One payment device identifies the whole rail journey. Each passenger has to use that device both times, because the system distinguishes a physical card from a card stored on a phone. Check the fare table before you travel, to compare contactless charging with purchasing a separate ticket. People who share a car will also need to account for petrol and parking.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Every rail journey also has a maximum time, and a very long time between the initial and final touch may result in two maximum fares. If a passenger could not touch correctly for a reason beyond their control, they may ask for a refund, and a journey history can show which card paid the fare. A visitor deciding whether to drive through busy traffic or use public transport can check these payment rules beforehand. One idea is to compare the time with a trip by bike, including time spent booking or waiting.

R_H3.passageTitle: Taking a bicycle on public transport

passages.label: A
passages.text: TransLink serves the Vancouver region in Canada. Its guide explains when a passenger may go with a bicycle on public transport, including buses, the regional metro and some other services. Someone who uses a motorbike needs a different plan. Even for a larger bicycle, special rules can affect the choice of service.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Each regular bus has a front rack with space for two bicycles. If both positions are occupied, the result can be a wait for another bus. A cyclist arranging a connection should keep some time free for that possibility, especially when busy traffic can slow the next service.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The cyclist is responsible for loading and unloading the bicycle. TransLink provides eleven places where people can practise using a rack, and a passenger should not ride a bicycle inside a station, on a platform or at a bus loop. Keeping the bicycle clean and free of sharp edges also protects other passengers. Slowly moving a bicycle when loading helps avoid an accident involving another passenger.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Bicycles can go on SkyTrain, SeaBus and West Coast Express, but each service has its own limits. On the Canada Line, one bicycle is allowed in each car. On the Expo and Millennium Lines, two are allowed in each car, and a busy train may have no room, so the passenger may need to take a later one.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A passenger may take a ferry with a bike at the beginning of a journey, pay for a ticket and continue into the countryside by rail. Someone else may drive because of congestion at the arrival point or the lack of a continuous pavement. A person who prefers to ride or go on foot still needs to check the connections, since busy services have finite capacity and people must share space with other passengers and their equipment. A delay can create a different result in cost or time, so frequent travellers compare what they spend on several parts of the trip.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A visitor sees ordinary bicycles on a bus and assumes any bike will be carried. Which facts should the visitor take into account?
options: Any bicycle can go on the bus if several people have already brought one.
A bus rack has room for a limited number, and a larger bicycle can be subject to other rules.
Bus racks are given as the reason motorbikes have the same rules as bicycles.
Apart from choosing a route, visitors need no information about their particular vehicle.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A bus comes but each position on the rack is occupied. What follows from the article?
options: The driver will have to make space for another bicycle immediately.
Later buses cannot use the same rack until the next day.
Any planned connection should be treated as unchanged.
The cyclist may need to wait for a later bus and allow for the delay.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which person is responsible for putting the bicycle on and taking it off?
options: The first person waiting at the bus loop
Someone working at a station exit

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why are both the condition of a bicycle and the way it is moved relevant when other people are nearby?
options: Only the ticket should stay clean and equipment can be moved however the rider wants.
Moving quickly is the only precaution an experienced rider needs.
Keeping it in a safe condition and moving it carefully can help protect people sharing the space.
The eleven practice places are provided to decide who is responsible for paying a fare.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How could the named rail lines affect two cyclists hoping to go together in one car?
options: Both lines take the same number whatever the level of demand.
One line's rule may leave room for only one of them per car, while another allows two if space is available.
The names of the lines determine who can put a bicycle on a bus rack.
All services will make a separate car available to the two passengers.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which statement compares what can happen on a bus and on a train when many people travel?
options: A full rack can delay a bus passenger, and a busy train can also leave no room for a bike.
Only the train requires sharing space, since the bus has unlimited capacity.
If a bus has space for a bike, every train has at least as much space.
Bicycles can go on any full vehicle as long as the rider has paid.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What does the example of starting on water and going on by rail show?
options: The payment for the first stage automatically establishes a place on every later service.
People must do all portions of a trip using the same type of vehicle.
Once the ferry has departed, the time of the next service can no longer matter.
Someone can use different services on one trip, so connections are worth checking.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A person has learnt to use the rack. What two other parts of a plan could still matter?
options: Practising with a rack means the other services no longer have limits.
The route will run on time whenever all cyclists know how to load their bikes.
Allow extra time if the bus rack is full and check how many bikes can go on the intended rail service.
Use practice time to avoid checking any conditions until after the journey.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A traveller wants to cycle just before boarding and again after arriving. Which two parts of the journey may require a change to that plan?
options: A cyclist cannot ride through the station, and traffic or gaps in the pavement near the destination may affect the later choice.
The person can ride freely in every station, and the pavement must be continuous outside it.
Someone who has a rail ticket can cycle on the platform and then use every road without traffic.
Only the type of ferry matters because stations and streets follow the same riding rules.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which conclusion fits the whole article about planning a trip with a bicycle?
options: Decide only from the cost of the first ticket, since the rest of the trip is fixed.
Plan to handle the bicycle yourself, check the rules for each stage and allow extra time where space may be limited.
Pick the first service because any payment ensures the bicycle can travel.
Assume every vehicle can carry the same number of bicycles and makes the same demands on riders.
